prize_parts.citation: for the development of the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength concept to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, enabling new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I keep B036 as my single preferred part, with Katori and Ye, and I have not changed my configuration since round 1. After the full exchange, the case rests on three things I can weigh as an instrument builder. First, one conceptual step (the magic wavelength, which removes the trap as the limiting systematic) was turned into a working many-atom standard. Second, the 10^-18 level has been reproduced and cross-compared by several independent laboratories, which is the confirmation I ask for before any claimed result. Third, the consequences are concrete and measurable: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, searches for drifts of constants and for dark matter, and relativistic geodesy. Five of eight members now name the same configuration with the same two names, and the round-1 files show that this agreement did not come from counting votes. Each of the five gives the same physical argument independently, including Johansson, who started with B036 in seventh place. I answer the chair's first question as follows. I think the novelty objection can be written into the citation by naming the object recognised: a many-atom optical lattice clock whose uncertainty is set by the atom and not by the trap. That is the distinction from the 2005 comb (a tool for counting optical cycles) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems and single-ion clocks). It is not a claim that precision metrology is new.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes. A citation can state the distinction, but a sceptical reader may still see an increment on recognised metrology. The attribution record is the second weakness. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, and the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN groups lie outside a two-name credit, and several members, myself included, are relying on recollection and not on a checked archive. I would want that history verified by the committee's expert reviewers before a final vote, and I do not regard a recollection-based answer as sufficient to close the question on its own. I also have not resolved whether the pending redefinition of the second should be awaited. My leaning is that it affects timing and not merit, but a committee that wanted the practical consequence demonstrated first could reasonably wait.

responses.point: Johansson moved B036 from seventh to first. He says the comb and ion-clock prizes make it look like an extension of rewarded metrology, and he finds the early priority history among Katori, Ye, Lemonde and others unsettled.
responses.response: Your move from seventh to first is the most informative single change in round 1, because you started from the objection that most worries me. The chair's question to you stands: does the answer given by Kroll and Lindroth settle it? I do not think it needs to be settled by argument alone. The prior prizes honoured an enabling tool (the comb) and control of single quantum systems (2012). A many-atom lattice clock is, in the device sense you care about, a controllable many-body system measured to a part in 10^18. If you accept that, I propose we put it in the citation wording. On priority, I agree that we cannot settle it from the supplied names. I would ask you, as the member who is least committed to metrology as a field, whether the allocation to Katori and Ye is one you would defend publicly, or whether you hold it only because your colleagues in atomic physics do.

responses.point: Kroll calls B036 the one candidate where evidence, maturity and attribution all line up, and he warns that his own ranking is biased toward measurement tools and should be discounted against discovery-type claims.
responses.response: I appreciate the bias disclosure, and I make the same one: as a detector builder I also lean toward tools. That is a reason to test our reasoning against the discovery-type candidates and not to drop it. I think B036 passes that test, because the claim is a measurement result that has been reproduced and that gives new bounds on physics, not just a better instrument. I am less comfortable with your statement that attribution is clean. Two names are clean only relative to the supplied list. You and I both flag Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow, and I would not call the allocation clean until an expert reviewer checks the priority record. On the second redefinition we both left the question open. I now lean toward treating it as a timing question and not a merit question, which is where Johansson, Lindroth and Olsson already stand.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B022 as a model-then-experiment case reproduced in many laboratories, concedes that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and that Cao and the other 2018 first authors cannot be credited, and lists B036 and B054 as safer if interpretation must settle first.
responses.response: I rely on you and Bernhard Mehlig for condensed matter, so I take your account of the physics as given, and I find the model-then-experiment structure persuasive. My difficulty is the criterion you yourself list in the case against. If settled interpretation is the test, B036 passes it and B022 does not yet. You treat the open pairing mechanism as a risk worth taking, and I can see the argument for it. But a three-name allocation that already leaves out Cao and the other first authors, together with an unresolved mechanism, makes B022 harder to defend in one citation than B036 is today. You keep B036 as your alternative. I would like to know whether any new fact about B036 would stop you from joining it, or whether the main thing keeping you at B022 is timing. If it is timing, I think the committee can say that B022 is a strong candidate for a later year without prejudice.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022 but says the maturity objection is serious, since the experimental discovery is only eight years old whereas B036 is older, better settled and widely supported, and he withdrew his earlier two-name proposal in favour of a three-name credit.
responses.response: I appreciate that you state the maturity problem plainly and that you list B036 as your first alternative, since it makes it possible to find ground we share. I also take your concession on Bistritzer as settling the allocation if B022 were to advance. The disagreement between us seems narrower than the vote count suggests: you and I agree that B036 is the more mature case, and we differ on whether maturity should decide this year. As chair I need to ask what finding on B022 would move you. For my part, I would be willing to revisit B022 favourably if the pairing mechanism or the nature of the correlated insulators became better established. I would not put it ahead of B036 now, only because of how long reproduction has had to accumulate, not because I judge its science to be weaker.

responses.point: Olsson supports B036 with the argument that it is an original invention, experimentally verified, that opens a door, and she notes she holds a Fellowship at the University of Tokyo, where Katori is based, without believing recusal is needed.
responses.response: I agree with your test of an invention that has been verified and that opens a door, and I use it myself. On the disclosure, I take your judgement that no recusal is needed, since you describe no collaboration with Katori. I will record in my own note that I see no conflict on this point. I would not like to see your first-ranked B021 lost, however. You decline to push it while the Urban credit is unchecked, which seems right to me, but the same standard should apply to B036: if the priority record among Takamoto, Katori and the other lattice-clock groups cannot be checked, we are applying a stricter bar to B021 than to B036. I would be reassured if you, as someone who is used to historical priority questions in instrument development, could say whether the RIKEN and JILA record supports Katori for the concept and first realisation.

uncertainties: Whether the priority history among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups supports exactly two names; my answer so far is from recollection, not from a checked record.

Whether the citation wording separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes clearly enough to satisfy a sceptical reader, which is the central objection from Johansson and the other B036 supporters.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing; I lean to timing, not merit, but have not resolved it.

For B012 and B022, whether source confirmation (KM3NeT, Baikal-GVD) or an understanding of the twisted-bilayer pairing mechanism will arrive soon enough to change the comparison. I cannot judge the condensed-matter candidates in depth and rely on colleagues and expert reviewers.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B036 is apparent from my profile, and I am not aware of any tie to Katori, Ye, JILA or RIKEN. Following the round-1 discussion I hold the same position as before. I work in astroparticle physics and detector development (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur), so I am a field neighbour of the IceCube candidate (B012) and the Event Horizon Telescope candidate (B055), and I would raise that proximity again if either became the leading proposal. I have also noted Olsson's disclosure about the University of Tokyo and see no reason for recusal. I do not judge the condensed-matter candidates myself.
